speaker: John McCain
text: Well, let — let me say, Bob, thank you.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, what about the citizen that stayed in their homes? That paid their mortgage payments? It doesn’t help that person in their home if the next door neighbor’s house is abandoned. And so we’ve got to reverse this. We ought to put the homeowners first. And I am disappointed that Secretary Paulson and others have not made that their first priority.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Senator Obama?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, first of all, I want to thank Hofstra University and the people of New York for hosting us tonight and it’s wonderful to join Senator McCain again, and thank you, Bob.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Would you like to ask him a question?

speaker: John McCain
text: No. I would like to mention that a couple days ago Senator Obama was out in Ohio and he had an encounter with a guy who’s a plumber, his name is Joe Wurzelbacher.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Is that what you want to do?

speaker: John McCain
text: That’s what Joe believes.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He has been watching ads of Senator McCain’s. Let me tell you what I’m actually going to do. I think tax policy is a major difference between Senator McCain and myself. And we both want to cut taxes, the difference is who we want to cut taxes for.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Now, the conversation I had with Joe the plumber, what I essentially said to him was, “Five years ago, when you were in a position to buy your business, you needed a tax cut then.”

speaker: John McCain
text: You know, when Senator Obama ended up his conversation with Joe the plumber — we need to spread the wealth around. In other words, we’re going to take Joe’s money, give it to Senator Obama, and let him spread the wealth around.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: OK. Can I…

speaker: John McCain
text: We’re not going to do that in my administration.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: If I can answer the question. Number one, I want to cut taxes for 95 percent of Americans. Now, it is true that my friend and supporter, Warren Buffett, for example, could afford to pay a little more in taxes in order…

speaker: John McCain
text: We’re talking about Joe the plumber. OBAMA: … in order to give — in order to give additional tax cuts to Joe the plumber before he was at the point where he could make $250,000.

speaker: John McCain
text: Nobody likes taxes. Let’s not raise anybody’s taxes. OK?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I don’t mind paying a little more.

speaker: John McCain
text: The fact is that businesses in America today are paying the second highest tax rate of anywhere in the world. Our tax rate for business in America is 35 percent. Ireland, it’s 11 percent.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Let’s go to another topic. It’s related. So if you have other things you want to say, you can get back to that.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, first of all, I think it’s important for the American public to understand that the $750 billion rescue package, if it’s structured properly, and, as president, I will make sure it’s structured properly, means that ultimately taxpayers get their money back, and that’s important to understand.

speaker: Schieffer
text: But you’re going to have to cut some of these programs, certainly.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Absolutely. So let me get to that. What I want to emphasize, though, is that I have been a strong proponent of pay-as- you-go. Every dollar that I’ve proposed, I’ve proposed an additional cut so that it matches.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And some of the cuts, just to give you an example, we spend $15 billion a year on subsidies to insurance companies. It doesn’t — under the Medicare plan — it doesn’t help seniors get any better. It’s not improving our health care system. It’s just a giveaway.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, thank you, Bob. I just want to get back to this home ownership. During the Depression era, we had a thing called the home ownership loan corporation.

speaker: John McCain
text: But — OK. All right.

speaker: Schieffer
text: The question was, what are you going to cut?

speaker: John McCain
text: Energy — well, first — second of all, energy independence. We have to have nuclear power. We have to stop sending $700 billion a year to countries that don’t like us very much. It’s wind, tide, solar, natural gas, nuclear, off-shore drilling, which Senator Obama has opposed.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Which ones?

speaker: John McCain
text: I have fought against — well, one of them would be the marketing assistance program. Another one would be a number of subsidies for ethanol.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: John McCain
text: … including $3 million for an overhead projector in a planetarium in his hometown. That’s not the way we cut — we’ll cut out all the pork.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, look, I think that we do have a disagreement about an across-the-board spending freeze. It sounds good. It’s proposed periodically. It doesn’t happen.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And we are now looking at a deficit of well over half a trillion dollars.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Do either of you think you can balance the budget in four years? You have said previously you thought you could, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: Sure I do. And let me tell you…

speaker: Schieffer
text: You can still do that?

speaker: John McCain
text: Yes. Senator Obama, I am not President Bush. If you wanted to run against President Bush, you should have run four years ago. I’m going to give a new direction to this economy in this country.

speaker: Schieffer
text: In four years?

speaker: John McCain
text: … reduce this — I can — we can do it with this kind of job creation of energy independence.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, there’s a lot of stuff that was put out there, so let me try to address it. First of all, in terms of standing up to the leaders of my party, the first major bill that I voted on in the Senate was in support of tort reform, which wasn’t very popular with trial lawyers, a major constituency in the Democratic Party. I support…

speaker: John McCain
text: An overwhelming vote.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I support charter schools and pay for performance for teachers. Doesn’t make me popular with the teachers union. I support clean coal technology. Doesn’t make me popular with environmentalists. So I’ve got a history of reaching across the aisle.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right…

speaker: John McCain
text: Let me just say, Bob.

speaker: Schieffer
text: OK. About 30 seconds.

speaker: John McCain
text: OK. But it’s very clear that I have disagreed with the Bush administration. I have disagreed with leaders of my own party. I’ve got the scars to prove it.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right.

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama, your argument for standing up to the leadership of your party isn’t very convincing.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. We’re going to move to another question and the topic is leadership in this campaign. Both of you pledged to take the high road in this campaign yet it has turned very nasty.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Obama, your campaign has used words like “erratic,” “out of touch,” “lie,” “angry,” “losing his bearings” to describe Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, this has been a tough campaign. It’s been a very tough campaign. And I know from my experience in many campaigns that, if Senator Obama had asked — responded to my urgent request to sit down, and do town hall meetings, and come before the American people, we could have done at least 10 of them by now.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up. All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, look, you know, I think that we expect presidential campaigns to be tough. I think that, if you look at the record and the impressions of the American people — Bob, your network just did a poll, showing that two-thirds of the American people think that Senator McCain is running a negative campaign versus one-third of mine.

speaker: John McCain
text: It’s not true.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: It absolutely is true. And, now, I think the American people are less interested in our hurt feelings during the course of the campaign than addressing the issues that matter to them so deeply.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, if you’ll turn on the television, as I — I watched the Arizona Cardinals defeat the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Congratulations.

speaker: John McCain
text: Every other ad — ever other ad was an attack ad on my health care plan. And any objective observer has said it’s not true. You’re running ads right now that say that I oppose federal funding for stem cell research. I don’t.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I mean, look, if we want to talk about Congressman Lewis, who is an American hero, he, unprompted by my campaign, without my campaign’s awareness, made a statement that he was troubled with what he was hearing at some of the rallies that your running mate was holding, in which all the Republican reports indicated were shouting, when my name came up, things like “terrorist” and “kill him,” and that you’re running mate didn’t mention, didn’t stop, didn’t say “Hold on a second, that’s kind of out of line.”

speaker: John McCain
text: You’ve got to read what he said…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Let — let — let… MCCAIN: You’ve got to read what he said.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Let me — let me complete…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … my response. I do think that he inappropriately drew a comparison between what was happening there and what had happened during the civil rights movement, and we immediately put out a statement saying that we don’t think that comparison is appropriate.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We can have serious differences about our health care policy, for example, John, because we do have a difference on health care policy, but we…

speaker: John McCain
text: We do and I hope…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … talking about it this evening.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: But when people suggest that I pal around with terrorists, then we’re not talking about issues. What we’re talking about…

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, let me just say I would…

speaker: Schieffer
text: (inaudible)

speaker: John McCain
text: Let me just say categorically I’m proud of the people that come to our rallies. Whenever you get a large rally of 10,000, 15,000, 20,000 people, you’re going to have some fringe peoples. You know that. And I’ve — and we’ve always said that that’s not appropriate.

speaker: John McCain
text: … unacceptable. So the point is — the point is that I have repudiated every time someone’s been out of line, whether they’ve been part of my campaign or not, and I will continue to do that.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, look, Bob, as I said…

speaker: Schieffer
text: I mean, do you take issue with that?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: You know, here’s what I would say. I mean, we can have a debate back and forth about the merits of each other’s campaigns. I suspect we won’t agree here tonight.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And what is important is making sure that we disagree without being disagreeable. And it means that we can have tough, vigorous debates around issues. What we can’t do, I think, is try to characterize each other as bad people. And that has been a culture in Washington that has been taking place for too long. And I think…

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, Bob, you asked me a direct question.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Short answer, yes, short answer.

speaker: John McCain
text: Yes, real quick. Mr. Ayers, I don’t care about an old washed-up terrorist. But as Senator Clinton said in her debates with you, we need to know the full extent of that relationship.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. I’m going to let you respond and we’ll extend this for a moment.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Bob, I think it’s going to be important to just — I’ll respond to these two particular allegations that Senator McCain has made and that have gotten a lot of attention.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, again, while you were on the board of the Woods Foundation, you and Mr. Ayers, together, you sent $230,000 to ACORN. So — and you launched your political campaign in Mr. Ayers’ living room.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s absolutely not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: And the facts are facts and records are records.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And that’s not the facts.

speaker: John McCain
text: And it’s not the fact — it’s not the fact that Senator Obama chooses to associate with a guy who in 2001 said that he wished he had have bombed more, and he had a long association with him. It’s the fact that all the — all of the details need to be known about Senator Obama’s relationship with them and with ACORN and the American people will make a judgment.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Let’s go to the next topic and you — we may want to get back into some of this during this next discussion. I want to ask both of you about the people that you’re going to bring into the government. And our best insight yet is who you have picked as your running mates.

speaker: Schieffer
text: So I’ll begin by asking both of you this question, and I’ll ask you to answer first, Senator Obama. Why would the country be better off if your running mate became president rather than his running mate?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, Joe Biden, I think, is one of the finest public servants that has served in this country. It’s not just that he has some of the best foreign policy credentials of anybody. And Democrats and Republicans alike, I think, acknowledge his expertise there.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, Americans have gotten to know Sarah Palin. They know that she’s a role model to women and other — and reformers all over America. She’s a reformer. She is — she took on a governor who was a member of her own party when she ran for governor. When she was the head of their energy and natural resources board, she saw corruption, she resigned and said, “This can’t go on.”

speaker: Schieffer
text: Do you think she’s qualified to be president?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: You know, I think it’s — that’s going to be up to the American people. I think that, obviously, she’s a capable politician who has, I think, excited the — a base in the Republican Party.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Do you think Senator Biden is qualified?

speaker: John McCain
text: I think that Joe Biden is qualified in many respects. But I do point out that he’s been wrong on many foreign policy and national security issues, which is supposed to be his strength.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Let’s go to — let’s go to a new topic. We’re running a little behind.

speaker: John McCain
text: Climate change.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Climate change, yes — has said what both of you have said, and, that is, we must reduce our dependence on foreign oil.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Can we reduce our dependence on foreign oil and by how much in the first term, in four years?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I think that in ten years, we can reduce our dependence so that we no longer have to import oil from the Middle East or Venezuela. I think that’s about a realistic timeframe.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Now I just want to make one last point because Senator McCain mentioned NAFTA and the issue of trade and that actually bears on this issue. I believe in free trade. But I also believe that for far too long, certainly during the course of the Bush administration with the support of Senator McCain, the attitude has been that any trade agreement is a good trade agreement. And NAFTA doesn’t have — did not have enforceable labor agreements and environmental agreements.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, you know, I admire so much Senator Obama’s eloquence. And you really have to pay attention to words. He said, we will look at offshore drilling. Did you get that? Look at. We can offshore drill now. We’ve got to do it now. We will reduce the cost of a barrel of oil because we show the world that we have a supply of our own. It’s doable. The technology is there and we have to drill now.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Let me respond. Actually, I understand it pretty well. The history in Colombia right now is that labor leaders have been targeted for assassination on a fairly consistent basis and there have not been prosecutions.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, let me just said that that this is — he — Senator Obama doesn’t want a free trade agreement with our best ally in the region but wants to sit down across the table without precondition to — with Hugo Chavez, the guy who has been helping FARC, the terrorist organization.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right, let’s go to a new topic, health care. Given the current economic situation, would either of you now favor controlling health care costs over expanding health care coverage? The question is first to Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We’ve got to do both, and that’s exactly what my plan does.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, it is a terribly painful situation for Americans. They’re seeing their premiums, their co-pays go up. Forty-seven million Americans are without health insurance in America today.

speaker: John McCain
text: Now, Senator Obama, I’d like — still like to know what that fine is going to be, and I don’t think that Joe right now wants to pay a fine when he is seeing such difficult times in America’s economy.

speaker: Schieffer
text: So that’s your objective?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: It is not and I just described it…

speaker: John McCain
text: No, you stated it.

speaker: John McCain
text: Excuse me.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I just described what my plan is. And I’m happy to talk to you, Joe, too, if you’re out there. Here’s your fine — zero. You won’t pay a fine, because…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Zero, because as I said in our last debate and I’ll repeat, John, I exempt small businesses from the requirement for large businesses that can afford to provide health care to their employees, but are not doing it.

speaker: Schieffer
text: What about that?

speaker: John McCain
text: Hey, Joe, you’re rich, congratulations, because what Joe wanted to do was buy the business that he’s been working for 10-12 hours a day, seven days a week, and you said that you wanted to spread the wealth, but — in other words, take Joe’s money and then you decide what to do with it.

speaker: John McCain
text: I want to leave money in your pocket. I want you to be able to choose the health care for you and your family. That’s what I’m all about. And we’ve got too much government and too much spending and the government is — the size of government has grown by 40 percent in the last eight years.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. A short response.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Very briefly. You all just heard my plan. If you’ve got an employer-based health care plan, you keep it. Now, under Senator McCain’s plan there is a strong risk that people would lose their employer-based health care.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Let’s stop there and go to another question. And this one goes to Senator McCain. Senator McCain, you believe Roe v. Wade should be overturned. Senator Obama, you believe it shouldn’t.

speaker: John McCain
text: I would never and have never in all the years I’ve been there imposed a litmus test on any nominee to the court. That’s not appropriate to do.

speaker: Schieffer
text: But you don’t want Roe v. Wade to be overturned?

speaker: John McCain
text: I thought it was a bad decision. I think there were a lot of decisions that were bad. I think that decisions should rest in the hands of the states. I’m a federalist. And I believe strongly that we should have nominees to the United States Supreme Court based on their qualifications rather than any litmus test. Now, let me say that there was a time a few years ago when the United States Senate was about to blow up. Republicans wanted to have just a majority vote to confirm a judge and the Democrats were blocking in an unprecedented fashion.

speaker: Schieffer
text: But even if it was someone — even someone who had a history of being for abortion rights, you would consider them?

speaker: John McCain
text: I would consider anyone in their qualifications. I do not believe that someone who has supported Roe v. Wade that would be part of those qualifications. But I certainly would not impose any litmus test.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I think it’s true that we shouldn’t apply a strict litmus test and the most important thing in any judge is their capacity to provide fairness and justice to the American people.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: So this is going to be an important issue. I will look for those judges who have an outstanding judicial record, who have the intellect, and who hopefully have a sense of what real-world folks are going through.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: John McCain
text: Obviously, that law waived the statute of limitations, which you could have gone back 20 or 30 years. It was a trial lawyer’s dream.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Yes, let me respond to this. If it sounds incredible that I would vote to withhold lifesaving treatment from an infant, that’s because it’s not true. The — here are the facts.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We should try to reduce these circumstances.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Let’s give Senator McCain a short response…

speaker: John McCain
text: Just again…

speaker: Schieffer
text: … and then…

speaker: John McCain
text: Just again, the example of the eloquence of Senator Obama. He’s health for the mother. You know, that’s been stretched by the pro-abortion movement in America to mean almost anything.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Let’s stop there, because I want to get in a question on education and I’m afraid this is going to have to be our last question, gentlemen.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: This probably has more to do with our economic future than anything and that means it also has a national security implication, because there’s never been a nation on earth that saw its economy decline and continued to maintain its primacy as a military power. So we’ve got to get our education system right. Now, typically, what’s happened is that there’s been a debate between more money or reform, and I think we need both.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, it’s the civil rights issue of the 21st century. There’s no doubt that we have achieved equal access to schools in America after a long and difficult and terrible struggle.

speaker: John McCain
text: We need to encourage programs such as Teach for America and Troops to Teachers where people, after having served in the military, can go right to teaching and not have to take these examinations which — or have the certification that some are required in some states.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Do you think the federal government should play a larger role in the schools? And I mean, more federal money?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, we have a tradition of local control of the schools and that’s a tradition that has served us well. But I do think that it is important for the federal government to step up and help local school districts do some of the things they need to do.

speaker: Schieffer
text: What about that, Senator?

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, sure. I’m sure you’re aware, Senator Obama, of the program in the Washington, D.C., school system where vouchers are provided and there’s a certain number, I think it’s a thousand and some and some 9,000 parents asked to be eligible for that.

speaker: John McCain
text: But to have a situation, as you mentioned in our earlier comments, that the most expensive education in the world is in the United States of America also means that it cries out for reform, as well.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I’ll just make a quick comment about vouchers in D.C. Senator McCain’s absolutely right: The D.C. school system is in terrible shape, and it has been for a very long time. And we’ve got a wonderful new superintendent there who’s working very hard with the young mayor there to try…

speaker: John McCain
text: Who supports vouchers.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … who initiated — actually, supports charters.

speaker: John McCain
text: She supports vouchers, also.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: But the — but here’s the thing, is that, even if Senator McCain were to say that vouchers were the way to go — I disagree with him on this, because the data doesn’t show that it actually solves the problem — the centerpiece of Senator McCain’s education policy is to increase the voucher program in D.C. by 2,000 slots.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right.

speaker: John McCain
text: Because there’s not enough vouchers; therefore, we shouldn’t do it, even though it’s working. I got it.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, thank you again, Bob.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I want to thank Senator McCain and Bob for moderating.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Obama, Senator McCain, thank you very much.
